summary:
## Ukulele Sizes Overview

The four most popular ukulele sizes, from smallest to largest, each offer a distinct feel and sound:
- **Soprano:** The smallest standard size, known for its classic, bright, and trebly ukulele sound. Its small body and neck make it very portable but can be challenging for players with larger hands.
- **Concert:** A bit larger than the soprano, with a longer and wider neck. It produces a fuller sound with more mid-range and better intonation up the neck.
- **Tenor:** Larger than the concert, offering even more volume, bass, and mid-range. The longer neck provides more space between frets, making it comfortable for both chords and single-note melodies.
- **Baritone:** The largest of the four, with a deep, bassy tone similar to a tenor guitar. It has a significantly different tuning than the other three sizes.

## Sound & Tone Characteristics

A fundamental principle for all instruments, including the ukulele, is that **the smaller the body, the higher the pitch**. As you move from the small-bodied soprano to the large-bodied baritone:
- **Soprano:** Sounds very bright and **trebly** due to the limited space for sound to resonate.
- **Concert:** Introduces more **mid-range** and **bass** for a fuller, more balanced tone.
- **Tenor:** Has a powerful sound with even more **bass** and **volume**.
- **Baritone:** The most **bassy** of the group, with a rich, deep sound.

## Tuning Variations

- **Standard Tuning (GCEA):** The soprano, concert, and tenor ukuleles are typically tuned to **G-C-E-A** (4th to 1st string).
- **High-G vs. Low-G (Tenor):**
  - **High-G (re-entrant tuning):** The traditional setup where the 4th (G) string is tuned higher than the 3rd (C) string. This creates the classic, bright strumming sound but limits the instrument's melodic range.
  - **Low-G (linear tuning):** A popular alternative where the 4th string is tuned an octave lower. This provides an extended bass range, which is excellent for playing scales and more complex melodies.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Baritone ukulele has a different tuning: D-G-B-E.** This tuning matches the top four strings of a standard guitar. Because of this, standard ukulele chord charts and lessons (for GCEA tuning) will not work for a baritone. You must find baritone-specific learning materials.

## How to Measure a Ukulele

To determine a ukulele's size, you measure its **scale length**, which is the distance from the **nut** (at the top of the neck) to the **saddle** (on the bridge).

- **Soprano:** ~13-14 inches
- **Concert:** ~14-15 inches
- **Tenor:** ~17 inches
- **Baritone:** ~19 inches

## Choosing the Right Ukulele for You

Consider these factors when selecting a ukulele:
- **Hand Size:** Players with larger hands may find the wider fret spacing of a **tenor** more comfortable. Players with smaller hands might prefer a **soprano** or **concert**.
- **Desired Sound:** Do you want the traditional bright sound (**soprano**) or a deeper, fuller tone (**tenor** or **baritone**)?
- **Playing Style:** While all sizes can be strummed, the added space and better intonation of **concert** and **tenor** ukuleles make them better suited for playing single-note melodies.

> [!NOTE]
> The **concert ukulele** is recommended as a safe and versatile choice for beginners, as it balances portability, comfortable playability, and a full sound.

> [!TIP]
> If possible, visit a music store to hold and play different sizes. The physical feel of the instrument is a crucial factor that you can only experience in person.

## Introduction to Ukulele Sizes

In this ukulele tutorial, we're going to talk about the different sizes and sounds of ukuleles, mainly the four most popular ones: the soprano, concert, tenor, and the baritone. I'm going to show you how to measure the ukulele and I'm also going to help you figure out which one is best for you.

## The Soprano Ukulele

Now let's start with the one, the smallest one we're going to talk about at least. This is a soprano or the standard ukulele. They do get a little bit smaller than this, they do have a sopranino or the pocket one, but really this is the one that we want to focus on here, because when they start getting too small, they just don't sound great and they also don't intonate well. So we have soprano. Let's listen to the sound for a second.

So a general rule with not only ukuleles but all instruments is the smaller the body, the higher the pitch. Now, that doesn't mean the volume, although our ears perceive that when it's a higher pitch, it's louder, but no, we're talking about just simply the pitch. This is simply because we don't have a lot of body here for that sound to resonate in, so these tend to sound a little bit more trebly.

Now, these have a very small body and also a very small neck. The soprano ukuleles are great because they're easy to hold, they're light, but they really sound best just for strumming chords. It's really the best thing for them because you don't have a lot of space and also just because, like I've mentioned, they even start to get out of tune as you move up the neck. So this is a soprano. Let's check out the next one up.

## The Concert Ukulele

So next, we have the concert, and you can see compared to the soprano, it's just got a little bit of a bigger body and a little bit of a longer neck. Let's see how this one sounds.

Now the bigger body of the concert produces a little bit more mid-range and a little bit more bass, and that's going to be typical as we move up to the different sizes. Also, the neck is a little bit longer and just a little bit wider too. So these sound great not only for chords, but also for some single notes. These also intonate better as you move up the neck. That means they stay in tune better. Sometimes the sopranos, even a smaller ukulele, they start getting out of tune when you move up the neck.

So the concert is a great choice because it's a little bit bigger than the soprano, and I like the sound a little bit better. And it's still small enough where it's easy to hold, but yet it still sounds like a really traditional ukulele as well. So the concert is a great one. Let's take a look at the tenor next.

## The Tenor Ukulele (High-G)

So here we have a tenor ukulele and a concert ukulele. So you'll notice the difference in the body. The tenor has a little bit of a bigger body. It's also a little bit wider as well, and then the neck is a little bit longer. Let's see how this one sounds.

The tenor, again, because of not only the bigger body but also the wider body, is going to produce even more mid-range, more bass. It's actually a little bit louder, even though because of the lower sound we don't perceive it as louder, but it's a little bit louder as well. Also the longer neck is really nice because it gives you that great option of chords, but also the single notes.

Now this particular tenor has a high G, and that means the 4th string—so one, two, three, four—is a high note. A lot of the soprano, the concerts especially, and then some of the tenors have a high G. That's really traditional sounding for ukulele. The only thing is you are a little bit limited because you have a first string as a high note, second string is a little bit lower, third gets a little bit lower, but then you have this high note. So you're almost really limited in the range of it. It sounds great, especially when you're strumming, but notice the single notes sound a little bit funny when we play it, right? It is okay, but it sounds a little bit off because you're coming from a low note to a really high note.

## The Low-G Tenor Ukulele

So this is a high G, but they do have what's called a low G. Let me show you that. So this is a tenor as well, but this one has a low G. And in that four strings, so now if you have the first string, second, third, and then fourth, it has that extra low note which gives it a little bit more range. So notice now when we do a scale, you had that extra note.

Now these are becoming really popular. This is what I play a lot of times because it gives you a little bit of extra range which is really nice, 'cause you're not limited now to three strings, you have that extra four string. Well when you strum it, it still sounds good. It's just gonna sound a little bassier. Check this out.

## The Baritone Ukulele & Its Unique Tuning

And then the last ukulele that I want to talk about today is the baritone ukulele. So here we have the baritone ukulele versus a tenor ukulele, and you can see the baritone has a bigger body. Also, it's a little bit wider, and then also the longer neck. Let's see how this one sounds.

Now this one is really bassy. This is actually the size of a tenor guitar. It does have the four strings, so it is a ukulele. The thing to also keep in mind with the baritone is that the tuning, the strings are different than they are on the soprano, the concert, and the tenor. So for example, on this baritone, the first string here is E, second string is B, third string is G, and then the fourth string is D. But now if you go back to the tenor, the first string is A, second string is E, third string here is C, and then fourth string is G. So keep that in mind because most stuff you see online, most lessons, most ukulele books are written for the concert, the soprano, and the tenor. So make sure if you have a baritone you want to look for things that are specifically written for the baritone. Now, I think these sound great, they're really cool sounding, but they are very bassy. And then with that different tuning, this is something you've got to watch out for.

## How to Measure Ukulele Scale Length

So now I want to talk about how you would measure a ukulele. You're simply going to measure from the nut down to the bridge, but more specifically the saddle. So simply just grab your tape measure, just put it down, and you notice that this tenor here is 17 inches. That's the length of it. The sopranos are going to run between 13 and 14 inches, it's gonna vary from company to company. The concert is going to be 14 to 15 inches. And then the baritone is gonna be 19 inches. So as you start extending the length, what happens, it starts allowing for the string to get longer, which gives you some low notes. And as we mentioned, also the body and the size of the ukulele also help determine that sound.

## How to Choose the Right Ukulele For You

What ukulele is right for you? There's many different choices out there between the four different sizes that we talked about. There's also all kinds of different woods, from solid woods to laminate woods, to koa wood, to spruce wood. They have plastic ukuleles, they have all different color ukuleles. So let's talk about size though. For me, I really would stick with a concert ukulele. I prefer the tenors, but I think the concert's a nice way to go because it's not too big, it's not too small. It's great for an instrument that you can strum chords and also play some single notes.

You also have to figure out, you know, how tall are you? If you're 6'5" and have huge hands, probably a tenor is going to be better for you. If you're really small and have small hands, then you want to maybe think about a soprano or a concert ukulele. So there's a lot of variety out there. I would recommend if you can go somewhere where they have different ones to try it out. Even if you don't even know what you're doing, just pick it up, hold it, touch the neck. You you'll feel it even if you don't even know how to play a chord or anything. And then if you do know how to play something, just play a few chords, play something simple, because playing it, feeling it, hearing it is going to help you decide what you want. But if you're just ordering online and you don't really know what you're getting, I gotta mention, I always stick with a concert. I think that's a real safe bet. And then, you know, if you want to expand out to a tenor, down to a soprano, that's cool. And then remember the baritone has that different tuning, so only get that if you really know specifically that you want the baritone.

## Conclusion

So anyway, we talked about the different sizes, the different sounds, how to measure them, maybe what's right for you. I hope this helped. There's a lot of really cool ukulele companies out there making a lot of really cool instruments, so you have a lot of variety. So it's a really exciting time to become a ukulele player.
